summary: Describes a protocol for carrying accounting information between a Network Access Server and a shared accounting server, which is used to record usage of network services. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RADIUS Accounting tells a central server when a user starts and stops using a network service, and how much the user used. The network access server sends short start and stop records, and the server acknowledges each one it stores. Operators use these records to bill and audit usage.

questions: what port does radius accounting use
what is a network access server
subtitle: How a network access server reports who used what service, and for how long, to a central accounting server.

tldr.problem: Network operators running dial-in and modem pools need a central record of the service each user received, but the RADIUS protocol only covered authentication and authorization.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Access Server sends Accounting-Request packets over UDP to a RADIUS accounting server, authenticated by an MD5 hash over a shared secret, and the server replies with an Accounting-Response only after it records the request.
tldr.outcome: The protocol became the standard way RADIUS carries usage records; RFC 2866 obsoletes RFC 2139 and is updated by RFC 2867, RFC 5080, RFC 5997 and RFC 9765.

today: RFC 2866 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 2139. It has been updated by RFC 2867, RFC 5080, RFC 5997 and RFC 9765, and has not been obsoleted itself.

sections.title: Extending RADIUS to Accounting
sections.content:
Managing dispersed serial line and modem pools for large numbers of users takes significant administrative support, and those pools need careful attention to security, authorization and accounting. The RFC says this is best achieved by managing a single database of users that handles authentication and holds configuration for the service to deliver, such as SLIP, PPP, telnet or rlogin.

The RADIUS protocol (RFC 2865) covers authentication and authorization. This memo extends RADIUS to carry accounting information from the Network Access Server (NAS) to a RADIUS accounting server. The NAS operates as a client: it passes accounting records to a designated server, which confirms that it received them. The accounting server can also act as a proxy client to other kinds of accounting servers.

The RFC highlights three features. A client/server model. Network security through a shared secret that is never sent over the network. And an extensible protocol: every transaction is made of variable-length Attribute-Length-Value triples, so new attribute values can be added without disturbing existing implementations. This memo obsoletes RFC 2139.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS already checked who a user was. This memo adds the part that records what service the user got, so an operator has one central list of usage instead of logs scattered across access servers.

sections.title: Start, Stop and Retries
sections.content:
When service delivery begins, the client generates an Accounting-Request that describes the type of service and the user, and the server sends back an acknowledgement that it received the packet. When service ends, the client generates a second Accounting-Request describing the service delivered and, optionally, statistics such as elapsed time, input and output octets, or input and output packets. Each service the NAS provides to a user is a session; each session generates a separate start and stop record with its own Acct-Session-Id.

The client should keep trying to send the Accounting-Request until it receives an acknowledgement, using some form of backoff, and can forward requests to alternate servers when the primary is down or unreachable. Retry and fallback algorithms are described as the topic of current research and are not specified in detail.

If the server cannot successfully record the accounting packet, it MUST NOT send an Accounting-Response. A server may also act as a client towards other servers. In the proxy arrangement the RFC sketches, a forwarding server may log the request, appends its own Proxy-State after any others, updates the Request Authenticator and forwards it; a forwarding server MUST NOT modify existing Proxy-State or Class attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: The server writes a record when a user starts and another when the user stops. If no acknowledgement arrives, the client keeps resending. If the server cannot store a record, it stays silent rather than claiming success.

sections.title: Packet Format and Types
sections.content:
Exactly one RADIUS Accounting packet is carried in the data field of a UDP datagram, and the UDP destination port is 1813 (decimal). Replies reverse the source and destination ports. Early deployments used UDP port 1646, which conflicts with the sa-msg-port service, so the officially assigned port is 1813.

The packet starts with a one-octet Code, a one-octet Identifier, a two-octet Length and a 16-octet Authenticator, followed by attributes. The codes are 4 for Accounting-Request and 5 for Accounting-Response. An invalid Code means the packet is silently discarded. Length covers the whole packet; a packet shorter than Length says MUST be silently discarded, octets beyond Length are padding and ignored, the minimum length is 20 and the maximum is 4095.

The Identifier matches requests with replies; the server can detect a duplicate request from the same client address, port and Identifier within a short span of time. The Identifier MUST change when the attributes change, and MUST stay the same for identical retransmissions. An Accounting-Request MUST carry either NAS-IP-Address or NAS-Identifier, and MUST NOT carry User-Password, CHAP-Password, Reply-Message or State. An Accounting-Response needs no attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record is one UDP message with a short header: a packet type, a matching number, the packet length and a 16-byte security stamp. Requests go to port 1813, and replies use the same header fields.

sections.title: Authenticators and the Shared Secret
sections.content:
The NAS and the accounting server share a secret, which is never sent over the network. In an Accounting-Request the Request Authenticator is a 16-octet MD5 checksum over a stream made of the Code, Identifier and Length, 16 zero octets, the request attributes and the shared secret. The RFC notes this cannot be done the way an Access-Request authenticator is done, because an Accounting-Request has no User-Password attribute.

The Response Authenticator in an Accounting-Response is a one-way MD5 hash over the response Code, Identifier and Length, the Request Authenticator from the request being answered, the response attributes if any, and the shared secret. The client matches the Identifier with a pending request, checks the Response Authenticator, and silently discards invalid packets.

One consequence the RFC spells out: when Acct-Delay-Time is present, retransmitting updates that value, which changes the attribute content and therefore requires a new Identifier and Request Authenticator. The Security Considerations section is brief: security issues are the authenticators and the shared secret described above.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides compute a stamp from the packet and a secret they share but never transmit. A matching stamp shows the packet came from the other side and was not changed.

sections.title: The Accounting Attributes
sections.content:
Each attribute has a one-octet Type, a one-octet Length and a Value. This memo defines types 40 to 51. Acct-Status-Type (40) marks the record as Start (1), Stop (2), Interim-Update (3), Accounting-On (7) or Accounting-Off (8); the last two let a client mark the start or end of accounting as a whole, for example around a reboot. Values 9 to 14 are reserved for tunnel accounting and 15 for Failed.

The usage counters are Acct-Input-Octets (42), Acct-Output-Octets (43), Acct-Input-Packets (47), Acct-Output-Packets (48) and Acct-Session-Time (46). All of these can appear only in records where the status is Stop. Acct-Delay-Time (41) says how many seconds the client has been trying to send the record. Acct-Session-Id (44) is a unique accounting ID so start and stop records for a session can be matched, and every Accounting-Request MUST have one. Acct-Authentic (45) says whether the user was authenticated by RADIUS, by the NAS itself, or by another remote protocol.

Acct-Terminate-Cause (49) gives one of 18 reasons a session ended, from User Request and Lost Carrier to Idle Timeout, Session Timeout and Host Request. Acct-Multi-Session-Id (50) links related sessions of one multilink session, and Acct-Link-Count (51) counts the links known to be in that session, so the accounting server can tell when it has received every Stop record for it. The table in the RFC shows which attributes may appear in an Accounting-Request; two attribute values are required: Acct-Status-Type and Acct-Session-Id, plus either NAS-IP-Address or NAS-Identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record carries labelled fields: start or stop, how long the session lasted, how many bytes and packets moved in each direction, why it ended, and an ID that ties the start and stop records together.

fields.name: Authenticator
fields.desc: 16 octets; Request or Response Authenticator, an MD5-based value.

messages.label: Accounting-Response
messages.note: Sent only if the record was recorded.

messages.label: Accounting-Request (Stop)
messages.note: Service ends; may carry time and octet counts.

items.label: Interim-Update
items.desc: Defined value for an update during the session.

items.label: Accounting-On
items.desc: Marks the start of accounting, for example upon booting.

items.label: Accounting-Off
items.desc: Marks the end of accounting, for example before a scheduled reboot.
